content: Acyclovir ointment is an antiviral medication approved by the FDA for the treatment of genital herpes and certain non-life-threatening mucocutaneous herpes simplex virus infections in immunocompromised patients. Common side effects include pain, swelling, itching, and rash. For adults, the FDA-approved use of Acyclovir ointment 5% involves applying enough ointment to cover all lesions every three hours, six times a day, for seven days. The amount applied should approximate a half-inch ribbon of ointment per four square inches of surface area. A finger cot or rubber glove should be used during application to prevent autoinoculation to other body sites and transmission to others. Treatment should begin as early as possible after the onset of symptoms. There is limited information regarding off-label uses of Acyclovir ointment in adults and pediatric patients. The FDA has not provided specific guidance for its use in pediatric patients, during pregnancy, labor, or delivery, or in nursing mothers. However, systemic exposure to Acyclovir following topical application is minimal. Nursing mothers with active herpetic lesions near or on the breast should avoid breastfeeding. Acyclovir ointment 5% is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to its components. It is intended for cutaneous use only and should not be applied to the eyes. In clinical trials, mild pain, including transient burning and stinging, was reported by approximately 30% of patients in both the active and placebo groups. Local itching occurred in 4% of patients. No significant differences in adverse reactions or abnormal laboratory findings were observed between the drug and placebo groups. Postmarketing reports include rare cases of edema, pain at the application site, itching, and rash. Acyclovir is a synthetic purine nucleoside analogue with selective inhibitory activity against herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 (HSV-1, HSV-2) and varicella-zoster virus (VZV). Its mechanism of action involves conversion by viral thymidine kinase into acyclovir monophosphate, which is further converted into its active triphosphate form. This active form inhibits viral DNA replication through competitive inhibition of viral DNA polymerase, incorporation into and termination of the growing viral DNA chain, and inactivation of the viral DNA polymerase. Resistance to Acyclovir can occur due to changes in viral thymidine kinase or DNA polymerase, particularly in immunocompromised patients. Clinical studies have shown that Acyclovir ointment 5% reduces healing time and, in some cases, the duration of viral shedding and pain in initial genital herpes infections. However, no clinical benefit has been demonstrated in recurrent genital herpes or herpes labialis in non-immunocompromised patients, although a reduction in viral shedding duration was observed. Each gram of Acyclovir ointment USP, 5%, contains 50 mg of Acyclovir in a polyethylene glycol base. It is supplied in 15 g and 30 g tubes and should be stored at 20°C to 25°C (68°F to 77°F). There is no established interaction between alcohol and Acyclovir ointment, but patients should consult their doctor regarding alcohol use while on this medication.
